cards.q: What is the key mental model for categorizing network devices across the course?
cards.a: Categorizing devices by their function as an end device or intermediary device, and by their plane (data, control, or management).

cards.q: What are end devices (hosts) and what identity do they have?
cards.a: End devices are PCs, laptops, phones, tablets, cameras, IoT, printers, and servers. They originate and consume traffic and have at least a MAC (L2) and typically an IP (L3) identity.

cards.q: At what layer does a hub operate and why is it avoided?
cards.a: A hub is a Layer 1 device that regenerates the signal to all ports, creating one collision domain, so it is legacy and avoided.

cards.q: What does a switch do and what data structures does it use?
cards.a: A switch at Layer 2/Layer 3 forwards frames by MAC using the CAM table, creates VLANs, provides microsegmentation, and an L3 switch routes between VLANs using the FIB.
A Layer 3 device performs path selection by IP using the routing table, interconnects networks, and can perform NAT and filtering.

cards.q: What does a wireless access point do?
cards.a: A Layer 2 device that bridges 802.11 RF frames onto the wired LAN, using BSSID association.

cards.q: What does a firewall do at L3-L7?
cards.a: A stateful firewall enforces policy, tracks sessions, and performs NAT with VPN/IPS capability.

cards.q: What does a load balancer do at L4-L7?
cards.a: It distributes flows across a server farm using a virtual IP (VIP) and heart checks.

cards.q: What is the role of a Wireless LAN Controller (WLC)?
cards.a: A WLC centralizes AP configuration, RF management, and roaming, operating in the management/control plane.
The actual forwarding path for user packets (frames/packets), running on ASICs/TCAM, with performance measured in pps/fib and using the switching fabric, TCAM/MAC table, and FIB.
The part that decides how to forward by building routing and forwarding tables, running routing protocols such as OSPF/EIGRP/BGP, and handling ARP/ND and STP.

cards.q: What is the management plane and what protocols does it include?
cards.a: The management plane is how the device is administered, using SSH/Telnet, SNMP, syslog, NTP, NetFlow export, and SDN controller connectivity via RESTCONF/NETCONF.

cards.q: Compare copper, fiber, and wireless physical media.
cards.a: Copper (UTP/STP) is cheap, short (up to 100 m), and susceptible to EMI and PoE capable; fiber is immune to EMI, with single-mode for long haul (laser) and multimode for short distances (LED/VCSEL); wireless (RF) offers mobility but a shared medium and interference.

cards.q: To which plane do STP and OSPF belong, and to which do forwarding ASIC decisions and SSH/SNMP belong?
cards.a: STP and OSPF belong to the control plane; forwarding decisions made in an ASIC belong to the data plane; and SSH/SNMP belong to the management plane.

cards.q: What layering distinguishes hubs, switches, routers, and firewalls?
cards.a: Hubs are Layer 1, switches are Layer 2 (plus Layer 3), routers are Layer 3, and firewalls are stateful Layer 4-7 devices.

cards.q: How is an L3 switch different from a WAN router?
cards.a: An L3 switch is a router for VLANs but not a WAN router, since it lacks the NAT/security focus; an SD-WAN edge is WAN CPE, not just a LAN switch.

cards.q: What is the difference between a router and a firewall?
cards.a: A router forwards traffic to connect networks, while a firewall is a security policy enforcement point performing stateful filtering. Both can perform NAT, but each is typical in its own location.

cards.q: Which command shows control-plane output (RIB) and which shows data-plane input (FIB/CEF)?
cards.a: show ip route shows control-plane output (the RIB), while show ip cef shows data-plane input (the FIB/CEF).

cards.q: What command identifies a device's version, model, and uptime?
cards.a: show version identifies the IOS version, model, and uptime; show ip interface brief shows L3 interfaces and their state; and show interfaces shows per-interface stats, errors, and duplex.
